demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
become overly compliant when feeling threatened
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't rely on other people
I can no longer trust my own body
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: 'Talks or photos about snakes' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another unless the accident specifically involved a snake, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other trigger items point to generic post-traumatic cueing, but this item implies a highly specific trauma cue that lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another and is not supported by the other nodes. The profile otherwise centers on guilt, danger scanning, intrusive recollection, and distrust of self/body; betrayal by another person introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme without corroboration.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Avoiding emotional closeness/intimacy is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The dominant threat and memory items concern danger, hypervigilance, intrusive imagery, numbness, and grief after an accidental injury event. Intimacy avoidance could occur, but here it appears to address an interpersonal/betrayal theme that is not otherwise coherently represented, especially given the unsupported betrayal appraisal.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by generalized interpersonal/environmental danger monitoring (avoiding unfamiliar places, scanning exits in any room), which fits assault or deliberate threat contexts better than accidentally causing serious injury to another in an accident. For this trauma type, threat is more plausibly focused on accidents, loss of control, or harm recurrence rather than pervasive escape-oriented vigilance across all settings.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I can't rely on other people' is weakly grounded in the rest of the profile. The other nodes center on accident-related triggers, guilt, bodily unreliability, and generalized hypervigilance, but there is no corresponding interpersonal betrayal, abandonment, or dependence theme to support this item. It stands out as clinically disconnected from the trauma narrative and the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Mina Tran was a 19-year-old hairdresser of Southeast Asian background who came to treatment after nearly a year of living with the aftermath of a road accident in which she had accidentally caused serious injury to another person. On the day of the event, she had been driving with a passenger when her attention was split for a moment and the car struck another vehicle. The details she could not shake were not abstract to her; they came back as sudden pictures of the impact, the other car hit by accident, and the sound that followed, especially any loud noise that seemed to cut through the room and drag her straight back to that instant. Since then, she had found herself jolted by the slam of a door in the salon, the sharp bang of equipment dropped on the tiled floor, or any unexpected crash from the street outside. Even when she knew she was safe, her body reacted as though danger had returned, and she described a constant inability to relax that made rest feel impossible.

In the hours and days after the accident, Mina kept replaying the scene in fragments. At times she could picture it with painful clarity, as though she were staring at a sequence of still images: the cars, the angle of impact, the moment everything went wrong. At other moments, she could recall what happened but felt strangely numb, as if it had happened to someone else, to a stranger she had been forced to watch from a distance. Then, without warning, the numbness would give way to overwhelming grief. What struck her most was not only what she had seen but what she felt she had done. She was convinced that she should have protected the other person and that she had failed. That belief settled into the way she spoke about herself, with a painful certainty that she could not undo what had happened and could not make herself the kind of person who would have prevented it.

Mina began avoiding anything that made the event feel close. She stopped driving entirely and would not ride as a passenger either, turning down lifts from her boyfriend and arranging her life so that she could get everywhere another way. Over time this narrowed the shape of her days. She worked as a hairdresser, and the salon became one of the few places she could still tolerate because it was familiar and predictable, but even there she entered each morning scanning the exits as soon as she walked in, noting where she could get out if something happened. She found herself listening for sudden sounds, her shoulders tightening at every bang or screech. When the calendar moved toward the date connected to the crash, she became especially guarded and tried to keep busy so she would not have to sit with the memory or the anniversary of what she had done. Those dates felt dangerous to her, not because she believed anything specific would happen, but because she feared being pulled back into the same helplessness and grief.

In the months after the accident, Mina also noticed how she behaved around people whenever she felt even slightly threatened. She became overly compliant, quick to agree, apologetic in a way that seemed almost automatic. At work, if a client sounded irritated, she would soften her voice, rush to please them, and make herself smaller rather than risk conflict. In her relationship, she worried that asking for too much might drive people away, and beneath that was a deeper conviction that she could not rely on other people anyway. The accident had left her with a sense that bodies could fail at any moment, including her own. She spoke of her body as if it were not dependable, something she could not fully trust to keep steady or respond correctly. That feeling sharpened whenever she noticed her heart racing or her muscles tensing after a loud noise or a sudden image of two cars colliding.

By the time she sought help, Mina was exhausted by the range of places she had to monitor herself: the salon, the street, the inside of a car, any room where she entered and immediately looked for an exit. She had grown tired of living in a state of alertness that never fully turned off and of carrying the grief of the accident in a way that surfaced whenever she remembered it. What brought her to treatment was the growing sense that her world had become too small and too carefully managed, and that she was frightened of spending the rest of her life organized around that one moment. What she hoped for, though she said it cautiously, was to be able to remember the accident without collapsing into shame or numbness, and to move through ordinary life without feeling as if danger were always one loud noise away.
